coverage: Nine stories · Outages, Spirit data sale, four-color algorithm, school search, youth friendships, Instagram, podcast captions, Canva, exam alerts

cards.headline: A week of outages: how experts tell glitches from cyberattacks
cards.summary: Within a week, a Microsoft outage, a US flight ground stop, a JPMorgan Chase payments bug and an NSA network problem hit in quick succession. There is no evidence they are linked or caused by hackers. Most were blamed on updates or upgrades that went wrong. One internet analyst told WIRED that only about one in a thousand outages he tracks turns out to be an attack. Investigators check status pages and internet-wide data on when and where failures began.
cards.whyItMatters: Big services depend on a few shared systems, so one bad update can ripple outward. Checking evidence before blaming hackers is the same habit as debugging: test the simplest cause first.

csp.connection: When many systems depend on one shared component, a single failure can cascade; redundancy reduces that risk.

cards.headline: Judge approves sale of Spirit Airlines workers' data to Google
cards.summary: A US bankruptcy judge approved Google's $10 million purchase of data from Spirit Airlines, which shut down in May. Google says it will use the data, including an estimated 100 million emails and half a billion Microsoft Teams messages, to train AI. After a union lawsuit, Google agreed to leave out health, drug-test and disciplinary records and to de-identify the data, meaning strip out details that point to specific people.
cards.whyItMatters: Messages you write at work or school can become valuable AI training data. A privacy expert warns that de-identified data can sometimes be linked back to people when combined with other information.

csp.connection: Removing names does not always make data anonymous; combining datasets can re-identify individuals.

cards.headline: Mathematicians find a much faster way to color any map
cards.summary: The Four Color Theorem says any flat map can be colored with four colors so neighboring regions never match. In 1976 it became the first major theorem proven with a computer. A six-person team now reports an algorithm that does the coloring in nearly linear time instead of quadratic time. They showed every map has many spots where coloring can start, not just one. The work will be presented at the FOCS computer science conference.
cards.whyItMatters: With the old method, a map with 10 times more regions took about 100 times longer. The new one takes only a little more than 10 times longer, which matters for huge inputs.

csp.connection: Algorithms that solve the same problem can differ hugely in efficiency as the input grows.

cards.headline: Big school districts weigh dropping Google Search over AI
cards.summary: The New York Times reported that, starting next year, schools that turn off Google's Gemini AI features would also lose Google Search. New York City and Chicago public schools said they may look for other search options, and Los Angeles is also considering alternatives. Google told The Verge it is piloting a step-by-step Guided Learning mode and that next year Gemini and Search will be off by default until schools choose what to enable.
cards.whyItMatters: Decisions like this shape which tools show up on your school Chromebook. It also shows how bundling features together can limit users' choices.

csp.connection: Design decisions by one company can affect millions of students, raising questions about choice and control.

cards.headline: Global survey: in-person friends linked to better well-being
cards.summary: Gallup and Boston Children's Digital Wellness Lab surveyed 15,925 people ages 15 to 22 in 16 countries. A median of 93% have a close in-person friend and 37% have a close online-only friend. In-person friendships were tied to higher life ratings; online-only ones were not. Short-form video scrolling, which 72% do often, was the only online activity linked to lower well-being. Those using AI as a companion reported more loneliness, but the study can't show cause.
cards.whyItMatters: The study describes people your age around the world. It shows patterns, not proof that any app causes loneliness, a difference worth keeping in mind with any survey.

csp.connection: Survey data can reveal correlations, but correlation alone does not prove one thing causes another.

cards.headline: Instagram now lets you edit a Story after posting
cards.summary: Instagram users can now fix text, music, stickers and drawings in a Story for up to 15 minutes after sharing it, Instagram head Adam Mosseri announced. Before, fixing a typo meant deleting and reposting, which lost views and replies and could scramble the order of a series. Edited Stories show an "edited" label. The feature is rolling out now.
cards.whyItMatters: Small design choices change how millions of people use an app. The "edited" label is a trade-off between letting people fix mistakes and keeping viewers informed.

cards.headline: SiriusXM and Pandora agree to transcribe podcasts for deaf listeners
cards.summary: SiriusXM agreed to provide podcast transcripts on SiriusXM and Pandora, settling a 2021 lawsuit brought under the Americans with Disabilities Act. Transcripts must identify speakers and include sound effects and proper punctuation. If speech-recognition software helps, a person must review the result. The company will also build custom word lists for each show.
cards.whyItMatters: Automatic captions still make mistakes, so human review matters. Accessible design lets more people join the same conversations.

csp.connection: Accessible design widens who can use technology; automated tools work best with human checks for accuracy.

cards.headline: Canva adds a switch to turn off its generative AI
cards.summary: Design platform Canva added a setting that turns off most generative AI tools, such as Magic Write and Magic Expand, for free and paid users. A second setting shows human-made templates and graphics first in its library. Background Remover and Magic Grab stay on, because Canva says they only rearrange what's already in a design rather than generating new content.
cards.whyItMatters: Many students use Canva for school projects. Being able to choose when AI helps gives you more control over your own work.

cards.headline: South Korea uses emergency phone alerts against exam cheating
cards.summary: South Korea planned to send a loud emergency-style alert to phones before Thursday's Suneung, an eight-hour college entrance exam taken by about 550,000 students, to expose hidden phones. Proctors will also check glasses for hidden cameras, and smart glasses are banned. The steps follow a man's admission that he photographed tax-exam questions with a tiny camera and fed them to an AI tool.
cards.whyItMatters: Schools everywhere are rethinking tests because of AI. It shows how a tool built for disasters can be reused for a very different goal.
